About · The Daily Grind

One reviewer. Six years. No paid placements.

The Daily Grind is a one-person espresso review blog, run from a kitchen in Portland, Oregon. Here's who writes it, how we test, and the long version of our affiliate disclosure.

The writer

Hi, I'm Greta.

I've been obsessed with espresso for fourteen years and a little bit annoying about it for about thirteen. I spent six years as a barista in Portland — three at Coava, two at Heart, one at Stumptown's Annex roastery — and one year as a green-coffee buyer for a small roaster in the Columbia Gorge. In 2018 I started writing reviews of home espresso gear because all the existing reviews seemed to be either rewritten manufacturer copy or breathless content from people who'd had the machine for two days.

I'm not a barista anymore. I'm a freelance writer who got obsessive enough about one specific topic that it now pays most of my rent. I make espresso every morning, write about it during the day, sometimes drink too much of it, and spend my weekends taking machines apart on the kitchen table to see how they work.

I live in Northeast Portland with my partner and two cats. The current home espresso bench is a Profitec Pro 300 + Niche Zero, but it rotates roughly every six weeks when a new machine comes in for testing. My partner is patient about this; the cats are not.

If you ever see me at a coffee shop, please come say hi. I am almost certainly drinking a cortado and reading something that has nothing to do with coffee.

How we test

Every machine reviewed on this site spends a minimum of 30 consecutive days as my primary kitchen-counter espresso machine. No exceptions, no expedited reviews, no "we tested for a week and here's our verdict." If I can't borrow a machine for the full window, it doesn't get reviewed.

The testing window

Thirty days, every day, on the same kitchen counter. Most days I pull two double shots — one for me, one for my partner — and steam milk for at least one cappuccino. Some days more. Across a 30-day window, every machine sees at least 60 espresso shots and 15 cappuccinos. Some see 100+.

What stays constant

The grinder (Niche Zero gen 3, dialed in fresh per bag), the water (RPavlis recipe, custom-mixed from distilled), the scale (Acaia Lunar), the rotation of beans (one light, one medium-dark, one dark). The grinder is single-dose and zero-retention, which means grinder variability is controlled for as much as is possible at home.

What changes

The machine. Only the machine. Recipes are re-dialed for each machine but every machine is tested against the same shot target — 18.5g in, 38g out, 30-second target, 93°C brew. Steam target is always 6 oz of 38°F whole milk to 140°F.

The five-axis rubric

Each machine is scored on shot quality (35%), temperature stability (20%), steam quality (20%), workflow and ergonomics (15%), and build quality / long-term outlook (10%). The weighting isn't arbitrary — it reflects what I think actually matters for someone spending their own money on a machine they'll live with for years.

What I don't test for

"Looks." App quality (when present). Brand prestige. Wireless features. Smart-home integration. None of these are wrong to care about; they just aren't what the site is for.

What you'll find here

  • Reviews based on at least 30 days of daily use
  • Buying guides updated at least twice a year
  • Opinions, including ones you'll disagree with
  • Mod guides and DIY upgrade walkthroughs
  • The occasional "I was wrong" post
  • Technical detail that assumes you can handle it
  • Comments open on every review; I answer most of them

What you won't find here

  • Sponsored posts or paid reviews. Ever.
  • Reviews of machines I haven't personally tested for 30+ days
  • Algorithmic best-of lists generated to chase search traffic
  • "Game-changing," "must-have," "you'll never look back"
  • Pod machines, super-automatics, or coffee robots
  • Discount codes for brands I haven't tested
  • Tracking that follows you off this site

Affiliate disclosure (long version)

Some — not all — of the retailer links on this site are affiliate links. That means when you click one and then buy the thing, I get a small commission from the retailer, at no extra cost to you. This is a real source of income for the site and is what makes it possible for me to spend 30+ days testing each machine without selling out the editorial.

Where I have affiliate relationships

I have affiliate accounts with: Amazon, Seattle Coffee Gear, Whole Latte Love, Clive Coffee, Prima Coffee, and Williams Sonoma. Commission rates vary by retailer and category — typically 2-6% of the sale.

What this changes about the reviews

Nothing. I have written negative reviews of machines sold by every retailer on that list, including the most-clicked machines on this site. If anything, I am paranoid about the appearance of bias and consequently more likely to score harshly.

How I buy test machines

Roughly half the machines I review I buy with my own money. The rest are loans from the manufacturer or from a retailer (typically with a return window of 60-90 days). When a manufacturer loans a machine, I disclose it in the review. I do not let manufacturers see the review before publication. I have, twice in the last six years, returned a loaned machine with a critical review attached; both manufacturers responded professionally. One has since fixed the problem I pointed out.

What I refuse

I refuse: paid sponsorships, paid placement in roundups, "sponsored posts" of any flavor, gifted machines I don't have to return, swag, expense-paid trips to factories. I have refused all of these. I will continue to refuse them. If a brand contacts me asking for paid coverage, I respond with a polite no and then put their product on my list to test honestly, at my own expense.

The honest summary

If you click a link on this site and then buy the thing, you support the site and don't pay any more for it. If you'd rather not, search the retailer directly — the review is the same either way. I'm not going to guilt-trip you about it.

Ethics statement

Quick version: I write about what I'd recommend to my brother.

If a machine is overpriced for what it does, I say so — even if I'm an affiliate of the retailer selling it. If a $499 machine outperforms a $2,000 machine in some meaningful way, I say that too. The bar for inclusion in a buying guide is "I'd be comfortable recommending this to a friend." The bar for the top of a buying guide is "I'd buy this with my own money tomorrow."

I do not accept paid reviews under any framing — including the new "we'll sponsor a six-month long-term test" pitches that started showing up in 2024. I do not write content for brand blogs or e-commerce sites. I do not appear in manufacturer-funded YouTube content. I have a day-job as a freelance writer that pays the rest of the bills; this site does not need to compromise to stay alive.

Contact

For readers: the comments section under each review is the fastest way to get a response from me. I read all of them and reply to most. For longer questions, email greta@thedailygrind.example — I answer within about a week.

For brands and PR: if you'd like a machine considered for review, please email reviews@thedailygrind.example with the product, the loan window you can offer, and a return-shipping label. I cannot guarantee timing or a positive review. I do not accept paid coverage of any kind.

For retailers: if a price on the site is outdated, please send the correction to greta@thedailygrind.example. I aim to update within 48 hours.

Mailing address: The Daily Grind, PO Box 14210, Portland, OR 97214.
